title: Reflog, bisect, and exact-snapshot investigation
outcome: Combine recovery and regression search without destroying unrelated working edits.
useCase: Regression investigations and accidental branch movements.
drawbacks: Historical environments and expired objects limit recovery/search.
version: Modern Git; check git --version for command availability
cue: Preserve work. Reproduce the symptom. Search the graph.

trace.title: Active edits preserved
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Use reflog to find a recent local reference movement, then name the candidate commit with a rescue branch before changing anything else.

Reflog is local and expires; it does not store every unsaved file.

Use bisect only after a repeatable good/bad check exists. A flaky network dependency can make a confident wrong culprit.

Verify the check against known endpoints of the search.

A worktree gives a separate checkout for the exact committed snapshot. It helps avoid accidentally testing a staged patch together with unstaged helper changes.

Save needed files before removing a worktree, and use Git’s worktree commands to keep registration consistent.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Observed regression → minimal deterministic check → known-good/bad commits → bisect or exact-snapshot comparison → inspect trigger → preserve regression test. Keep the active worktree’s edits untouched.

A first-bad dependency update is a trigger to investigate, not automatically the root explanation. Reproduce the mechanism after locating the change.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
A test can fail because its historical build environment is unavailable. Mark such commits untestable/skip rather than bad.

A cleanup command can delete untracked work that Git never stored.
